subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - North America Reading
subtitle: Reading passages on North America's regions, climates, settlement, resources, and sustainability.
description: Reading comprehension passages for the North America world regions pack. The passages use source-grounded case studies and interpretation questions about physical geography, climate, settlement, migration, resources, sustainability, and hazards.

data.sourceTitle: North America as a World Region
data.targetTitle: North America as a World Region
data.sourcePassage: North America is a large and varied world region. It includes Canada, the United States, Mexico, Central America, Greenland, and the Caribbean islands when studied broadly. Geographers sometimes use a narrower definition, so they always ask how a region is being defined. North America can be studied through physical geography, human geography, economic geography, and environmental geography. A fishing village in Greenland, a farming town in Kansas, a Caribbean island community, a desert city in Arizona, and a megacity in central Mexico all belong to the same world region, but they face different opportunities and challenges. This is why geographers compare subregions instead of assuming the whole continent is the same.

questions.question: Name three large countries included in North America.
questions.modelAnswer: Canada, the United States, and Mexico are three large countries included in North America.

questions.question: Which answer best defines a region?
questions.modelAnswer: A region is an area with shared features.

questions.question: Why do geographers pay attention to how North America is defined?
questions.modelAnswer: They pay attention because different definitions change what places, people, environments, and patterns are included in the study.

questions.question: How does the passage show that North America is diverse?
questions.modelAnswer: It contrasts places such as Greenland, Kansas, Caribbean islands, Arizona, and central Mexico to show different climates, settlements, economies, and challenges.

questions.question: Explain why subregions help geographers avoid oversimplifying North America.
questions.modelAnswer: Subregions let geographers compare places with similar features while still recognizing that climate, culture, economy, hazards, and daily life differ across the continent.

data.sourcePassage: North America's climate varies widely because the region covers many latitudes, elevations, landforms, and ocean influences. Northern places such as Greenland and northern Canada receive less direct sunlight and are colder, while southern Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean are warmer. Mountains also matter. Higher places are usually cooler than nearby lowlands, and mountain ranges can block moist air. This can create a rain shadow, where one side of a mountain receives more precipitation and the other side is much drier. Oceans can make coastal temperatures milder because water heats and cools more slowly than land. These patterns help explain why Phoenix, Arizona is hot and dry, while Montreal, Canada has colder winters and more even precipitation.

questions.question: What is a rain shadow?
options: A dry area on the side of a mountain away from moist winds
A storm that forms over the Great Lakes
A warm ocean current in the Caribbean
A city built beside a natural harbor
questions.modelAnswer: A rain shadow is a dry area on the side of a mountain away from moist winds.

questions.question: Why are northern Canada and Greenland colder than many southern parts of North America?
questions.modelAnswer: They are farther north, receive less direct sunlight, and include Arctic or subarctic environments.

questions.question: How can oceans affect nearby coastal climates?
questions.modelAnswer: Oceans can make coastal temperatures milder because water heats and cools more slowly than land.

questions.question: Use Phoenix and Montreal to explain the difference between climate and weather.
questions.modelAnswer: Phoenix's hot, dry pattern and Montreal's colder winters with more even precipitation describe climate because they show long-term patterns, not a single day's weather.

data.sourcePassage: People often settle where water, transportation, food, and jobs are available. In North America, many large cities developed near coasts, rivers, lakes, or natural harbors. New York City grew near the Atlantic Ocean and a major harbor, New Orleans near the mouth of the Mississippi River, Chicago near the Great Lakes, and Vancouver as a Pacific port city. However, physical geography can also create challenges. Arctic areas can be extremely cold and remote, desert cities must manage limited water, mountain areas can make roads and railways difficult to build, and hurricane-prone coasts need storm planning. Population is unevenly distributed, so high-density areas often include cities and transport routes, while low-density areas often include deserts, mountains, remote forests, and Arctic or subarctic regions.

questions.question: Why do natural harbors help cities grow?
questions.modelAnswer: Natural harbors make shipping and trade easier, which can attract businesses, workers, and infrastructure.

questions.question: Explain why a desert city may face a different challenge from a port city.
questions.modelAnswer: A desert city may have limited water and heat challenges, while a port city may focus on shipping, storm risk, pollution, and coastal planning.

questions.question: How does this passage show that physical geography creates both opportunities and challenges?
questions.modelAnswer: Water features can support trade, jobs, and city growth, but cold, deserts, mountains, and hurricane-prone coasts create planning and infrastructure challenges.

data.sourcePassage: North America has many natural resources, including fresh water, fertile soils, forests, fish, oil, natural gas, minerals, and renewable energy sources such as wind, solar, hydroelectric power, geothermal energy, and biomass. These resources support farming, mining, manufacturing, tourism, technology, and trade. The Great Plains and Canadian Prairies support grain and livestock, while California's Central Valley grows fruits, vegetables, nuts, and dairy with irrigation. Resources can create jobs and trade, but they can also raise sustainability questions. Irrigation can support crops in dry areas, but it may reduce river flow or groundwater levels. Fertilizers can increase yields, but runoff can pollute waterways. Tourism can bring income, but it can also pressure water, housing, reefs, beaches, and local communities.

questions.question: How can irrigation be both useful and challenging?
questions.modelAnswer: Irrigation helps crops grow in dry areas, but it can reduce river flow or groundwater levels if too much water is used.

questions.question: Why does tourism create sustainability questions?
questions.modelAnswer: Tourism can bring income and jobs, but it may also put pressure on water, housing, reefs, beaches, and local communities.

questions.question: Explain why resources do not automatically make a place wealthy or sustainable.
questions.modelAnswer: Resources can support jobs and trade, but benefits depend on management, technology, infrastructure, environmental protection, ownership, prices, and whether impacts are shared fairly.

data.sourceTitle: Case Studies: Rivers, Cities, the Arctic, and the Caribbean
data.targetTitle: Case Studies: Rivers, Cities, the Arctic, and the Caribbean
data.sourcePassage: Case studies help geographers connect general ideas to real places. The Mississippi River system drains a huge area and supports transportation, farming, cities, wetlands, and ports, but it also faces flooding, pollution, and wetland loss. The Colorado River Basin supplies water to cities, farms, dams, recreation, and ecosystems in a dry region, so drought and high demand create difficult choices. Mexico City is a large urban area in a highland basin, where jobs and culture are major opportunities but traffic, air pollution, water supply, and land subsidence are challenges. The Arctic is home to Indigenous communities and ecosystems affected by changing sea ice and melting permafrost. The Caribbean has beaches, reefs, ports, farms, and tourism, but hurricanes and storm surge require careful preparation.

questions.question: Why does the Colorado River Basin face difficult choices?
questions.modelAnswer: It supplies water to many users in a dry region, and drought plus high demand can make water sharing difficult.

questions.question: How can melting permafrost affect Arctic communities?
questions.modelAnswer: Melting permafrost can make buildings, roads, and other infrastructure unstable and can affect travel, wildlife, and community planning.
